C0.quote: We study the voting game where agents’ preferences are endogenous decided
C0.note: Binary majority vote with threshold; strategic and equilibrium analysis of voting.

C1.quote: every 𝜀-strong Bayes Nash Equilibrium with 𝜀 converging to 0
C1.note: Main results characterise ε-strong BNE (EQ). Fidelity analysis of strategy profiles, including informative and sincere voting, is coded WD: it measures performance against the informed majority decision.

C2.1.value: votes (each agent votes for A or R)
C2.1.quote: Each agent 𝑛 votes for A or R.

C2.2.quote: Each agent 𝑛 votes for A or R.
C2.2.note: Binary vote for one of two alternatives, possibly chosen by a mixed strategy contingent on a private signal.

C2.3.loc: Section 2, Utility and Types of Agents, p.4
C2.3.quote: Each agent 𝑛 has a utility which is a function
C2.3.note: Utilities over (state, outcome), endogenous preferences and private signals.

C2.4.quote: A (mixed) strategy is a mapping from the agent’s private signal
C2.4.note: Votes are strategies, with notation separate from the utilities v_n. The paper states agents may deviate from sincere or informative voting.

C3.1.quote: we study two common non-strategic behavior – informative voting
C3.1.note: The equilibrium analyses model strategic voters. The informative and sincere voting case studies fix behaviour.

C3.2.quote: A sincere agent chooses the alternative that maximizes the expected utility
C3.2.note: Sincere and informative behaviour are defined in words for the non-strategic case studies.

C3.3.quote: we study the two most common non-strategic voting schemes
C3.3.note: The behaviours are justified as common, and they serve as benchmarks against strategic voting.

C4.1.note: C2.2 is OTH only (binary votes), so the applicability condition is not met.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.loc: Section 2, Definition 3, p.6; Section 3, Example 5, p.8
C5.1.quote: Fidelity is the likelihood that the informed majority decision is reached.
C5.1.note: Fidelity measures how often the alternative favoured by the informed majority of voters is chosen. Expected utilities of agents are also evaluated (Fig. 1b).

C5.2.quote: the alternative favored by the majority of the agents
C5.2.note: Evaluated on utilities/preferences defined separately from votes.

VOT.quote_behav: apply the analysis to the most common forms of non-strategic voting
VOT.loc_info: Section 2, Utility and Types of Agents, p.4
VOT.quote_info: are common knowledge and do not depend on 𝑁
VOT.note: Voters have a private signal, a common prior, common-knowledge signal distributions and common-knowledge type fractions. Others' signals are unknown.

C8.1.loc: Section 2, ε-strong Bayes Nash Equilibrium, p.6
C8.1.quote: we use the solution concept of 𝜀-strong Bayes Nash Equilibrium

C8.2.quote: we use the solution concept of 𝜀-strong Bayes Nash Equilibrium

claims.quote: Our results give merit to strategic voting for making good decisions.
These observations indicate that strategic behavior “prevails” over non-strategic behaviors in binary voting!
We show that strategic voting always leads to the informed majority decision

C9.2.quote: we assume that various constraints in the real world prevent discussion
C9.2.note: The needed assumptions are stated: votes are distinct from utilities, agents are strategic and coalitional, the information structure (common prior and signals), no communication, and the restriction to regular profiles.
